chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad — all from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a young boy who had not reached maturity, a boy of ten years, who committed fornication with a woman. He said: 'The boy shall be flogged less than the full Hadd, and the woman shall receive the complete Hadd.' It was said to him: 'What if she was married?' He said: 'She shall not be stoned, because the one who copulated with her had not reached maturity; and if he had been mature, she would have been stoned.'

key_terms.الحد: Hadd — the fixed penalty prescribed in Islamic law for specific major offences such as fornication
key_terms.الرجم: Rajm — the penalty of stoning, reserved in classical Islamic law for the muhsan (married adult) who commits zina
key_terms.المحصنة: Muhsana — a married, free, adult Muslim woman; marriage status affects whether rajm (stoning) applies
key_terms.المدرك: Mudrik — one who has reached legal maturity (puberty/bulugh); determines full legal accountability

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling in Islamic law when a pre-pubescent boy commits fornication with a woman?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was asked about the legal ruling when a ten-year-old pre-pubescent boy commits fornication with a woman. The Imam ruled that the minor boy receives a reduced punishment (less than the full Hadd of flogging), while the adult woman receives the full Hadd. Furthermore, if the woman was married, she still does not receive the stoning penalty (rajm), because the application of rajm requires that the other party also be legally capable (i.e., adult and sane). This hadith reflects a core principle in Islamic jurisprudence that legal penalties (hudud) are contingent on the full legal capacity (taklif) of all parties involved, illustrating how the Imams applied careful jurisprudential reasoning to complex cases.
